quote: Newton’s discovery gave rise to the notion of a universal law, one that is the same everywhere and everywhen, with literally zero exceptions.
content: The notion predates Newton by at least a generation and its history is not what the essay says. Descartes’s Principia Philosophiae (1644) laid down three “laws of nature” explicitly framed as holding everywhere and always; the phrase and the concept go back through the medieval jurists and theologians to the Stoics (see Ruby (1986), Journal of the History of Ideas on the origin of “law” in science, and Milton (1981), Archives Européennes de Sociologie). Newton’s Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy inherit the concept; they do not invent it. And the man credited with the exceptionless law did not himself believe in exceptionless law: Newton held that the solar system was unstable under gravitation alone and that God intervened periodically to reform it (Opticks, Query 31), a position Leibniz ridiculed in the Leibniz–Clarke correspondence as making God a bad watchmaker. The clean picture of “universal law with literally zero exceptions” is Laplace’s, a century later. The essay’s history of the idea reverses who believed what, and it does so in the service of a moral about how counterintuitive universality is to humans, a moral that the actual history, with its Stoics, jurists and Cartesians, does not support.

quote: As far as we know, there has been not one single violation of Conservation of Momentum from the uttermost dawn of time up until now.
content: Conservation of momentum is a poor choice of exemplar for a law that holds “everywhere and everywhen,” because in the standard cosmological model it does not hold globally. By Noether’s theorem, momentum conservation follows from spatial translation invariance; an expanding Friedmann–Robertson–Walker spacetime is not translation-invariant in the required sense, and there is in general no conserved global energy–momentum in general relativity, only local conservation of the stress–energy tensor’s covariant divergence and, in special cases, quasi-local quantities that physicists still argue about (Hoefer (2000); the review by Szabados (2009) lists more than a dozen inequivalent definitions). The redshift of the cosmic microwave background is a loss of photon momentum with no compensating gain that anyone can locate. The essay could have said “local conservation laws hold in every interaction we have observed,” which is true; what it said instead is the eighteenth-century version, and the eighteenth-century version was superseded by the very theory the next paragraph uses as its example of a law that had been operating all along.

quote: For when the dust subsides and the old theory is overthrown, it turns out that the universe always was acting according to the new generalization we have discovered, which once again is absolutely universal as far as humanity’s knowledge extends.
content: The essay concedes the pessimistic meta-induction in passing (“or so our new model tells us”) and then proceeds as if it had not. The historical pattern the paragraph describes, every previous exceptionless law having turned out to be a limiting case of something else, is the premise of Laudan’s argument that current theories will meet the same fate (Laudan (1981)), and the essay’s own inductive habit, generalizing from history, licenses that conclusion at least as well as it licenses the Tao at the end. There are answers to Laudan (structural realism, Worrall 1989, keeps the mathematical structure while dropping the ontology), but they are answers, and the essay does not give one; it asserts that “the Law itself was always absolutely constant” while its only evidence is a sequence of models each of which was believed to be that Law. The 80% credence in the lightspeed limit is a healthier statement of the same thing, and it is a statement about a model, not about a Law. The rhetorical move from “our best model is exceptionless” to “reality is exceptionless” is the map–territory confusion the essay warns against, run in the direction the essay approves of.

quote: One of the reasons the ancient Greeks didn’t discover science is that they didn’t realize you could generalize from experiments. The Greek philosophers were interested in “normal” phenomena. If you set up a contrived experiment, you would probably get a “monstrous” result, one that had no implications for how things really worked.
content: This is false as history. Ptolemy’s Optics (Book V) reports measured refraction angles for air–water, air–glass and water–glass at ten-degree intervals, obtained with a purpose-built apparatus, and generalizes a rule from them; Strato of Lampsacus argued for the existence of small voids from experiments with air and water in sealed vessels; Erasistratus weighed a bird and its food and excreta to demonstrate insensible perspiration; Hero and Philo built pneumatic devices; Archimedes’s hydrostatics is a deductive theory checked against contrived setups; Aristotle himself describes the incubation-series dissection of chick embryos, a contrived experimental series if there ever was one. Lloyd’s Magic, Reason and Experience (1979, a book with no DOI) and his earlier survey (Lloyd, “Experiment in Early Greek Philosophy and Medicine,” Proceedings of the Cambridge Philological Society, 1964) document dozens of cases and show that the Greek limitation was the absence of a systematic tradition of experiment, not a belief that contrived results were “monstrous.” The “monstrous” idea belongs to Aristotle’s biology (terata, births against nature), not to his physics, and Bacon’s claim that the ancients despised experiment is Bacon’s polemic, which the essay repeats. Book I made the same error about Bacon and the origins of science; this is the Greek edition.
